claims.text: A physics-informed machine-learning model incorporating realistic defects and oxygen impurities can predict temperature-dependent electrical conductivity of bulk HfNbTaTiZr more accurately than current analytical models.
Current analytical conductivity models for HfNbTaTiZr are based on ideal, defect-free crystals.
The relevant material is bulk polycrystalline HfNbTaTiZr with typical processing-induced defects and up to approximately 1 wt.% oxygen.
The proposed model would be trained using experimental conductivity data, including data for specimens with 1 wt.% oxygen, and simulated structures containing realistic defect distributions.
Conductivity measurements for HfNbTaTiZr specimens containing 1 wt.% oxygen are available for use in model training.
Quantum and defect-induced localization effects may dominate conductivity behavior in the 0–200 K regime.
Phonon and impurity scattering control conductivity in the 300–1200 K regime.
Oxygen-induced defects and their interaction with the high-entropy microstructure modify the electronic density of states.
Oxygen-induced defects influence electron-scattering rates in HfNbTaTiZr.
Point defects, oxygen clusters, and associated localized states can be represented through data-driven adjustments of electron-scattering parameters.
Incorporating defect-related features allows the model to capture non-ideal effects omitted by perfect-crystal analytical theories.
Defect-aware modeling will capture enhanced electron scattering at low temperatures.
Defect-aware modeling will capture combined phonon and impurity scattering at high temperatures.
The proposed model will predict conductivity within approximately 10–20% of experiment across both stated temperature regimes.
Idealized analytical models typically deviate from measured conductivity by approximately 30% or more.
The predicted conductivity curves will reflect distinct scattering mechanisms in the low- and high-temperature regimes.
The model is applicable to bulk HfNbTaTiZr containing oxygen on the order of 1 wt.% within approximately 0–200 K and 300–1200 K.
Samples with substantially different oxygen contents or major processing-induced microstructural changes may fall outside the model's applicability.
Failure to observe a predicted transition in activation energy between the temperature regimes would falsify the proposed mechanism.
A conductivity error greater than 20% at any benchmark temperature would falsify the hypothesis.
